'''''Inga edulis''''', known as '''ice-cream bean''', '''paterna''', '''whitey, padoo, cushín''' (short variety), '''joaquiniquil''', '''cuaniquil''' (both from [[Nahuatl]]: ''cuahuxinicuile'' combining ''cuahuitl'' "tree"; ''icxitl'' "feet" and ''necuilli'' "crooked"<ref>{{cite book|first=Ricardo|last=Muñoz Zurita|language=es|title=Diccionario enciclopédico de la Gastronomía Mexicana|url=https://laroussecocina.mx/palabra/jinicuil-o-cuajinicuil/|date=2012|publisher=Larousse|isbn=978-607-21-0619-2}}</ref>) '''guama''', or '''guaba''', is a fruit native to Central and South America. It is in the [[Mimosoideae|mimosoid tribe]] of the legume family [[Fabaceae]].<ref name="6subfamilies">{{cite journal |author=The Legume Phylogeny Working Group (LPWG). |year=2017 |title=A new subfamily classification of the Leguminosae based on a taxonomically comprehensive phylogeny |journal=[[Taxon (journal)|Taxon]] |volume=66 |issue=1 |pages=44–77 |doi=10.12705/661.3|doi-access=free |hdl=10568/90658 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It is widely grown, especially by [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous]] Amazonians, for shade, food, timber, medicines, and production of the alcoholic beverage ''cachiri''. It is popular in [[Peru]], [[Ecuador]], [[Pernambuco]]-[[Brazil]], [[Venezuela]], [[Guyana]], [[Costa Rica]]   and [[Colombia]].<ref>Duke (1983)</ref> The taxonomic [[genus|generic]] name ''Inga'' is derived from its name with the [[Tupí people]] of South America (''ingá''<ref>{{cite web|language=pt|title=Ingá - Inga edulis|website=Arvores do Brasil|access-date=28 Apr 2023|url=https://www.arvores.brasil.nom.br/new/inga/index.htm}}</ref>) while the [[species|specific]] name ''[[wikt:edulis|edulis]]'' is Latin for "edible". The common name "ice-cream bean" alludes to the sweet flavor and smooth texture of the pulp.

== Biology ==
Mature trees of ''I. edulis'' reach 30 m (98 ft) high and 60 cm (2.0 ft) diameter at breast height, usually branching from below 3 m (9.8 ft). The branches form a broad, flat, moderately dense canopy. ''I. edulis'' can be evergreen in tropical regions or deciduous when planted in colder regions. The tree has a pale grey-coloured trunk. The stems and young twigs can be sparsely to densely haired. The leaves are alternate, evenly [[pinnate]], 10–30 cm long, with four to six pairs of opposite, dark-green, membranous, slightly pubescent, oval leaflets. The terminal leaflets can grow up to 18 cm long by 11 cm wide in comparison to the basal ones. Extrafloral [[nectaries]] are placed on [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]], and [[stipule]]s can be either inconspicuous, absent, or caducous.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=Edible Medicinal and Non-Medicinal Plants |chapter=Inga edulis |last=Lim |first=T. K. |date=2012 |pages=715–719 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |doi=10.1007/978-94-007-1764-0_80 |isbn=978-94-007-1763-3 }}</ref>

The flowers are fragrant, sessile, and pentamerous, and are arranged in dense axillary spikes. Each flower has a calyx tube with five puberulent, striated lobes, and a [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]] with five silky, villous petals. These are around 14–20 mm long and contain numerous white [[stamen]]s. The fruits are longitudinally ribbed, cylindrical, indehiscent, [[leguminous]] pods, which can be straight, curved, or often spirally twisted up. They are pendant and up to 1 m long and yellowish brown to green in colour. The number of purplish-black to olive-colored ovoid seeds can vary from 10 to 20. These are embedded in the sweet, cottony, white [[arillus]], which gives it the name ice-cream bean, since their texture and sweetness are reminiscent of ice cream.<ref name=":2" />

===Symbiosis===
''Inga'' species are symbiotic with ants (e.g., ''[[Pheidole]]'' species), which feed on the nectar of the extrafloral nectaries. In exchange, the ants patrol over the ''Inga'' plant to protect it against [[herbivore]]s. Certain insects, such as [[Riodinidae|Riodinid]] caterpillars, excrete sugary honeydew from their tentacle nectaries. The ants form a symbiosis with the caterpillars by letting them feed on the tree in exchange for their sugary honeydew.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cassidy |first=Josh |date=November 2016 |title=The Double-Crossing Ants to Whom Friendship Means Nothing |url=https://www.kqed.org/science/1089990/the-double-crossing-ants-to-whom-friendship-means-nothing |access-date=2 December 2018 |website=KQED}}</ref>

The inga plant can also form symbiotic relationships in which nitrogen gas can be fixated by [[rhizobia]]l bacteria and [[mycorrhiza]], as can other legumes. Surveys have shown that ''I. edulis'' forms a mutualistic relationship with  ''[[Bradyrhizobium]]'' bacteria.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Leblanc|first1=Humberto A.|last2=McGraw|first2=Robert L.|last3=Nygren|first3=Pekka|last4=Roux|first4=Christine Le|date=2005-08-01|title=Neotropical Legume Tree Inga edulis Forms N2-fixing Symbiosis with Fast-growing Bradyrhizobium Strains|journal=Plant and Soil|language=en|volume=275|issue=1–2|pages=123–133|doi=10.1007/s11104-005-0808-8|s2cid=1299107|issn=0032-079X|url=http://agritrop.cirad.fr/529698/|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Synonyms ==
This plant has a convoluted history of [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonymy]] with ''[[Inga vera]]''. The plants discussed under that name by [[John Patrick Micklethwait Brenan|Brenan]] and [[Carl Sigismund Kunth|Kunth]] are actually ''I. edulis'', whereas that based on the writings of [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]] refers to the actual ''I. vera''. ''Inga edulis'' in works referring back to authorities other than [[Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius|von Martius]] usually refers to ''[[Inga feuilleei]]''.<ref name=ildis2005>ILDIS (2005)</ref>{{Full citation needed|date=August 2025}}

== Ecology ==
[[File:Inga edulis 11.jpg|thumb|Pods]]
The natural distribution of ''I. edulis'' spreads from [[Central America|Central]] to South America, and ranges from subtropical dry to tropical wet conditions.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web|url=https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Inga_edulis.html#Distribution|title=Inga edulis|website=hort.purdue.edu|access-date=18 November 2018}}</ref> It can be found at elevations from sea level up to 2200 m. ''I. edulis'' grows best when mean annual daytime temperatures range from 23 to 30 °C. However, it can tolerate 18–35 °C. During the resting period, mature trees can survive −2 °C, while young plants are killed at 0 °C. Preferred [[precipitation|annual precipitation]] ranges from 1200 to 2500 mm but 640 to 4000 mm of annual precipitation can be tolerated, also. It can be grown on a widely varying range of soil conditions. It prefers a [[soil pH]] of 5.0–6.5, but can also grow in very strongly acidic soil down to a pH of 4.5 or moderately alkaline conditions up to pH 8.0.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/dataSheet?id=1260|title=Data sheet|website=ecocrop.fao.org|access-date=18 November 2018|archive-date=28 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230428020748/http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/dataSheet?id=1260}}</ref> The natural habitat includes margins of large rivers like the [[Amazon River|Amazon]], thickets below high water line, and wooded swamps.<ref name=":02" /> The tree can tolerate temporarily waterlogged soils for 2–3 months each year, but it can also tolerate drought seasons up to 6 months.<ref name="worldagroforestry" /> Furthermore, ''I. edulis'' can cope with heavy soils or slope fairly well.<ref name=":02" /> In terms of soil fertility, ''I. edulis'' is not only unpretentious, but also has the potential to improve [[soil quality]]. As a [[Fabaceae|leguminous tree]], this species can compensate for nutrient-depleted soils by [[Nitrogen fixation|fixing nitrogen]] with its root nodules. Ammonium and nitrate salts found in soil typically result in nodulation reduction. ''I. edulis'' is an exception, as its nodules increase in size when ammonium ion levels are at 5{{nbsp}}mM. Nitrate, though, did not benefit ''I. edulis'' and continued to show properties that prevented nodulation. Additionally to nitrogen, ''I. edulis'' is reported to significantly increase the extractable [[phosphorus]] content in the soil, thus further ameliorates degraded soils.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fisher|first=Richard F.|date=1995|title=Amelioration of Degraded Rain Forest Soils by Plantations of Native Trees|journal=Soil Science Society of America Journal|volume=59|issue=2|pages=544–549|doi=10.2136/sssaj1995.03615995005900020039x|issn=0361-5995|bibcode=1995SSASJ..59..544F}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Inga edulis-Mounts Botanical Garden.jpg|thumb|At [[Mounts Botanical Garden]]]]
''I. edulis'' is widely cultivated in [[agroforestry]] systems in its [[Neotropical realm|neotropical]] dispersal area. This form of cultivation, often associated with [[Coffea|coffee]] or [[Theobroma cacao|cocoa]] culture, is widely known since [[Pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian]] times.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Allen|first1=O. N.|title=The Leguminosae|date=1981|pages=1–704|publisher=Macmillan Education UK|isbn=978-1-349-06144-0|last2=Allen|first2=Ethel K.|author-link2=Ethel K. Allen|doi=10.1007/978-1-349-06142-6_1|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }}</ref> [[Germination]] of ''I. edulis'' seeds is fairly easy, as the seeds are recalcitrant and often germinate already in the pod. Seeds lose their ability to germinate, though, after two weeks of storage.<ref name="worldagroforestry" /> Direct sowing of the seeds is possible, but the establishment of seedlings with already a certain height can decrease [[Competition (biology)|competition]] with noxious weeds, thus increasing growth.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lojka, B., Preininger, D., Van Damme, P., Rollo, A., Banout J.|title=Use of the amazonian tree species INGA edulis for soil regeneration and weed control|journal=Journal of Tropical Forest Science|volume=24|pages=89–101}}</ref> Further, the inoculation with [[rhizobia]] and [[mycorrhiza]]l fungi in depleted soils is recommended to promote growth.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Genus Inga: Utilization|last=Pennington, T.D., Fernandes, E.C.M.|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew|year=1998|isbn=978-1-900347-58-7|pages=41–52}}</ref> These inoculi can easily be produced by collecting soil, nodules, and fine roots from mature, nodulated ''I. edulis'' stands.<ref name=":02" /> This species seems to be very resistant to pests and diseases. Minor damage can result from fungal attacks in the seedling stage. Mature ''I. edulis'' can be defoliated by [[Lepidoptera]] larvae. Also, fruit fly larvae often damage the seed testa. In [[Ecuador]], ''I. edulis'' is specially susceptible to [[mistletoe]] infestations.<ref name="worldagroforestry" />

'''Food crop'''
''I. edulis'' has been cultivated as a [[fruit tree]] for millennia,{{citation needed|date=May 2025}} and is widely sold on the local South American marketplace, mainly for the sweet, succulent pulp surrounding the seeds. The white pulp ([[aril]]) is consumed raw as a sweet snack, though it is less nutritious than the seeds. Toxic compounds such as [[trypsin]] and [[chymotrypsin]] inhibitors contained in the seeds of ''I. edulis'' are destroyed through cooking.<ref name=":2" />{{Nutritional value|name=Inga edulis seeds|kJ=494|carbs=24.0 g|fat=0.7 g|protein=10.7 g|fiber=1.6 g}}The taste is described as resembling that of [[vanilla ice cream]]. Some varieties even possess a slight cinnamon flavor.<ref name="pfaf">{{cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/User/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Inga+edulis|title=Inga edulis – Mart.|last1=Mart.|website=www.pfaf.org|access-date=18 November 2018}}</ref><ref name="worldagroforestry">{{cite web|url=http://www.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/speciesprofile.php?Spid=991|title=Inga edulis|website=www.worldagroforestry.org|access-date=18 November 2018}}</ref> The seeds are edible only when cooked and have a taste similar to that of [[chickpeas]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}}

In [[Colombia]], the arils are also used to prepare an [[alcoholic drink|alcoholic beverage]] called ''cachiri'' for a festival of the same name. The native women chew the arils and spit the mixture into a vat, where it is left to ferment.<ref name=":02" /> The fruit ripens quickly and can only be kept for three to four days, limiting potential export opportunities, but refrigeration can extend [[shelf life]] to about three weeks.<ref name="review2">{{cite journal|last1=Lojka|first1=B.|last2=Dumas|first2=L.|last3=Preininger|first3=D.|last4=Polesny|first4=Z.|last5=Banout|first5=J.|date=2010|title=The use and integration of Inga edulis in agroforestry systems in the Amazon – review article|url=http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=CZ2011000249|journal=Agricultura Tropica et Subtropica (Czech Republic)|volume=43|issue=4|pages=352–359|access-date=18 November 2018|issn=0231-5742}}</ref>

===Use in agroforestry systems===

Due to its rapid growth and ability to improve soil properties, ''I. edulis'' has found widespread use in tropical [[agroforestry]]. Most notably, [[inga alley cropping]] is used as an alternative to [[slash and burn cultivation|slash-and-burn cultivation]]. It is also a popular shade tree for [[coffee]], [[Cocoa bean|cocoa]], and [[tea]] plantations. One important reason for this is that in comparison to other [[shade tree]] species, ''I. edulis'' retains its leaves in the dry season.<ref name="review2" /><ref name="worldagroforestry" /> Cuttings and leaves are also used as mulch and animal fodder.<ref name="worldagroforestry" /> The wood is sometimes used as timber and for fuel; its popularity as a source of firewood stems from its high caloric value and weak smoke production.<ref name="pfaf" />

Despite its rapid growth and significant potential to improve soils in agroforestry systems, ''I. edulis'' has not been the object of any improved breeding programs.<ref name="review2" /> However, the plant has been shown to exhibit strong [[introgression]] with ''I. ingoides'' in species-contact areas. This could allow for selection of hybrids via interspecific [[Hybridity|hybridization]] to further increase yield and flood tolerance of the crop.<ref name="hybridization">{{cite journal|last1=Rollo|first1=A.|last2=Lojka|first2=B.|last3=Honys|first3=D.|display-authors=etal|date=2016|title=Genetic diversity and hybridization in the two species Inga ingoides and Inga edulis: potential applications for agroforestry in the Peruvian Amazon|journal=Annals of Forest Science|volume=73|issue=2|pages=425–435|doi=10.1007/s13595-015-0535-0|s2cid=18127015|url=http://repositorio.ipcb.pt/bitstream/10400.11/4656/1/Rollo%20AFS%202016%20uncorrected%20proof.pdf|doi-access=free|bibcode=2016AnFSc..73..425R }}</ref>

===Medicinal uses===

''I. edulis'' is widely used in native South American folk medicine. [[Decoctions]] of the leaves, bark, or root commonly are used as treatments for diarrhea, arthritis, and rheumatism.<ref name=":02" /> Crushed, boiled leaves are ingested to relieve coughing or applied to lip sores, possibly caused by [[herpes]].<ref name="pfaf" /><ref name=":2" /> Several studies have investigated ''I. edulis'' as a source of [[polyphenols]] for use as [[antioxidant]]s and
